t.3.29.1: Having shattered that mace with his arrows, Rāghava, devoted to dharma, smiled and spoke these vehement words to Khara.
t.3.29.2: This is the whole of your strength that you have shown, O vilest of rākṣasas. Far weaker in power than I, you roar in vain.
t.3.29.3: This mace of yours, shattered by my arrows, has fallen to the surface of the earth, destroying the confidence of you who are so bold in speech.
t.3.29.4: What you said, "I am wiping away the tears of the rākṣasas who have been slain," even that word of yours is false.
t.3.29.5: I shall snatch away the life-breaths of this base rākṣasa, mean in character and false in conduct, just as Garutmān carried off the nectar of immortality.
t.3.29.6: Today, when your throat has been cut and you have been torn apart by my arrows, the earth will drink your blood, adorned with foam and bubbles.
t.3.29.7: With all your limbs smeared with dust and both your arms slack and outflung, you will sleep embracing the earth as though she were a woman hard to win.
t.3.29.8: When you, the disgrace of the rākṣasas, lie sunk in deep sleep, these Daṇḍaka forests will become a refuge for those who have no refuge.
t.3.29.9: O rākṣasa, once Janasthāna, your abode, has been destroyed by my arrows, the sages will roam fearlessly everywhere in the forest.
t.3.29.10: Today the rākṣasa women, whose kinsmen have been slain, will scatter in every direction out of fear, wretched, their faces wet with tears, they who once brought terror to others.
t.3.29.11: Today, O night-wanderer, those wives of worthy family whose husband is such a one as you will come to know the taste of grief.
t.3.29.12: O you of cruel conduct, mean-souled one, ever a thorn to the brāhmaṇas! Because of you, the sages, filled with dread, cast their oblations into the fire.
t.3.29.13: As Rāghava, greatly enraged, spoke thus on the battlefield, Khara, his voice made harsher by fury, reviled him.
t.3.29.14: Surely you are exceedingly arrogant, and fearless even in the midst of dangers; and therefore, being in the power of death, you do not know what ought to be said and what ought not to be said.
t.3.29.15: Those men who are bound by the noose of Time do not know what should be done and what should not be done, for their six senses have been cast aside.
t.3.29.16: Having spoken thus to Rāma, the night-wanderer then knit his brows in a frown, and he saw a great sāla tree not far away.
t.3.29.17: Looking about on every side in the battle for a weapon, he bit his lip and tore it up by the roots.
t.3.29.18: Lifting it up with both arms, the mighty one roared, hurled it at Rāma, and cried, "You are slain!"
t.3.29.20: Then Rāma, drenched in sweat, the corners of his eyes red with rage, pierced Khara in battle with a thousand arrows.
t.3.29.19: Cutting it down with floods of arrows as it came hurtling toward him, the mighty Rāma summoned up fierce wrath in order to slay Khara in battle.
t.3.29.21: From the gaps between the arrows in his body much frothy blood flowed forth, like the streaming torrents of water pouring from a mountain spring.
t.3.29.22: Khara, made reeling in the battle by Rāma's arrows, yet maddened by the smell of blood, swiftly rushed at him alone.
t.3.29.24: Then, in battle, Rāma seized an arrow resembling fire for the slaying of Khara, like a second rod of Brahmā.
t.3.29.23: As he came rushing on, furious and drenched in blood, the one skilled in weapons, quick in his stride, drew back a little, step by step.
t.3.29.25: He, the righteous-souled one, fitted to his bow that arrow given by the wise Maghavan, king of the gods, and released it toward Khara.
t.3.29.26: That great arrow, loosed by Rāma after he had raised his bow, roaring like a thunderclap, fell upon the chest of Khara.
t.3.29.27: Burning in the fire of the arrows, Khara fell to the ground, like Andhaka consumed by Rudra in the White Forest.
t.3.29.28: Like Vṛtra struck down by the thunderbolt, like Namuci by the foam, or like Bala slain by Indra's lightning, Khara, slain, fell to the ground.
t.3.29.29: Then all the royal sages and the supreme sages, gathered together and filled with joy, honored Rāma and spoke these words.
t.3.29.30: For this very purpose the greatly splendid great Indra, Pākaśāsana, Puraṃdara, came to the holy hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
t.3.29.31: You were brought to this region by the great sages through a stratagem, for the purpose of slaying these cruel rākṣasas of sinful deeds.
t.3.29.32: Thus this task of ours has been accomplished by you, O son of Daśaratha; now the great sages will practise their dharma in happiness throughout the Daṇḍaka forests.
t.3.29.33: Meanwhile the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, together with Sītā, came out of the mountain stronghold and, happy, entered the hermitage.
t.3.29.34: Then the victorious hero Rāma, honoured by the great sages and saluted by Lakṣmaṇa, entered the hermitage.
t.3.29.35: Seeing him, the slayer of enemies and the bringer of happiness to the great sages, Vaidehī became joyful and embraced her husband.
